chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from Ali (peace be upon him), who said:
The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) sold the service of the Mudabbir, but did not sell his neck (freedom).

key_terms.الْمُدَبَّرِ: The Mudabbir (a slave manumitted upon paying a fixed sum)
key_terms.رَقَبَتَهُ: His neck (metonymy for his status of freedom/manumission)

ai.seo_question: What is the legal status of selling a Mudabbir's service versus his freedom in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights a nuanced distinction in Shia jurisprudence between the transferable service of a *Mudabbir* and the inalienable status of their eventual freedom. By clarifying that the Prophet sold the 'service' but not the 'neck,' it ensures the slave's path to manumission remains intact, reflecting the principle that the core right to liberty cannot be commodified. This ruling underscores the protective legal framework established for semi-free slaves within the early Islamic community.
